runtime_boundary: Represents the TensorRT LLM library and its trtllm-serve, trtllm-bench, and trtllm-eval tools, operated on GPUs the user controls. It is not TensorRT, the general-purpose NVIDIA deep-learning inference library and engine-builder it can compile through, and it is not NVIDIA's managed offerings, which hold their own serving contract and belong to the inference-service collection. NVIDIA Dynamo and Triton Inference Server orchestrate this engine and are separate boundaries, as is NVIDIA Model Optimizer, the offline quantization toolkit whose checkpoints this runtime loads.
model_management: Models are named by Hugging Face repository identifier or local checkpoint directory at engine construction, with a pluggable checkpoint-loading architecture that separates config loader, weight loader, and weight mapper so a new checkpoint format can be added without changing the engine. Pre-quantized checkpoints produced by NVIDIA Model Optimizer load directly; offline quantization is a separate step in that project. Multiple LoRA adapters are supported per request. There is no runtime model store, pinning, or removal command, and the legacy TensorRT backend additionally requires an engine build step whose artifact is specific to the GPU architecture and parallelism configuration it was built for.
hardware_requirements: The published support matrix limits the reviewed runtime to Linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with NVIDIA GPUs from the Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, Grace Hopper, and Blackwell architectures including GB200 NVL72; architectures outside that list are community-supported only. Available precisions vary by architecture, with FP8 documented from Ada Lovelace onward and INT4 AWQ or GPTQ with FP8 activations requiring compute capability 8.9 or higher. Windows and macOS are not supported, and a Jetson path exists only on a separate release branch.
operational_controls: Parallelism is configured at launch through tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data-parallel sizes, alongside KV-cache dtype and block reuse, chunked prefill, CUDA graph batch sizes, scheduler policy, and speculative decoding mode. trtllm-serve exposes /health, /metrics, and /version, with the metrics endpoint reporting runtime iteration statistics including GPU memory use and in-flight batching detail. Anonymous telemetry is collected by default and can be disabled by environment variable, a marker file, a Python config field, or a CLI flag. A stated deprecation policy gives a three-month migration window with runtime warnings.
strengths: Serving capability is unusually complete, covering in-flight batching, paged KV cache with block reuse, chunked prefill, an overlap scheduler, prefill-decode disaggregation, and tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism across single-node and multi-node deployments.

Quantization coverage is broad and documented per model, spanning NVFP4, MXFP4, several FP8 recipes, FP8 and NVFP4 KV cache, and W4A8 or W4A16 AWQ and GPTQ, with a published model-by-model support table.

The server implements OpenAI Chat, Completions, and Responses endpoints plus a dedicated embeddings subcommand with dynamic batching, alongside guided decoding, multi-LoRA serving, and multimodal input.
tradeoffs: Execution is confined to NVIDIA GPUs on Linux; there is no CPU, AMD, Apple, or Windows execution path in the reviewed support matrix, so the runtime cannot serve a mixed fleet.

The project carries two backends whose model coverage differs, and the current PyTorch backend is primary while the TensorRT engine-building path is documented separately, so a capability confirmed for one backend is not evidence for the other.

Several headline features are labelled beta or prototype in the documentation, including disaggregated serving and AutoDeploy, and the published support matrix page is stamped almost a year older than the installation guide, so version-specific verification is required.

The repository ships a visual-generation model directory under a restricted community license with revenue-based commercial terms, so redistribution and commercial use of the whole tree are not uniformly Apache-2.0.
license_note: The root LICENSE file states Apache-2.0 as the project license and then reproduces three further license texts covering code derived into the project from other open-source projects. Portions derived from CUTLASS, causal-conv1d, and flash-attention are BSD-3-Clause; portions derived from Bitcoin Core, flash-linear-attention, InstructEval, and MiniMax Sparse Attention are MIT; portions derived from FlashInfer, Mamba, Quack, SGLang, Text Generation Inference, Transformers, XGrammar, vLLM, and Baseten's suffix-automaton speculative decoding are Apache-2.0. The same file also reproduces the LTX-2 Community License Agreement, which the file scopes explicitly to tensorrt_llm/_torch/visual_gen/models/ltx2/ and which is not an open-source license: it requires entities with annual revenues of at least ten million dollars to obtain a separate paid commercial license, imposes use-based restrictions, and requires derivatives to be distributed under the same agreement. That directory exists in the repository and carries its own NOTICE pointing back to the root file. The Apache-2.0 core is therefore accompanied by a restricted component, which is why this record is classified open_core rather than mixed_open_source; GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the file opens with a custom header and concatenates four license texts.
